newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia vows peaceful tack on Khmer Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia vows peaceful tack on Khmer Rouge.

text.p: Cambodia will continue to use talk rather than force to try to persuade Khmer Rouge hardliners to defect, despite the failure of discussions with the rebels last month, top officials said on Friday.
"We hope that we will be able to resolve (the situation), even (in) Anlong Veng, without any fighting," First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters.
He was referring to the northern Cambodian stronghold of hardliners loyal to Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot.
Cambodian television meanwhile aired a speech by co-Premier Hun Sen saying hardliners in the capital Phnom Penh were ready to defect.
A spokesman for Hun Sen told Reuters on Friday that Hun Sen would meet the hardliners on Saturday afternoon. He declined to explain who the hardliners were or why they were in the capital.

Military analysts estimate that about 800 to 2,000 hardliners remain in the Anlong Veng stronghold on the Thai border. Hun Sen has predicted that the Khmer Rouge will be finished as a military power by mid-1997.

The Khmer Rouge, who under Pol Pot ran the genocidal 1975-1979 regime which killed more than a million people through disease, execution, torture or overwork, have been hit with massive defections in recent months.
Ieng Sary, Pol Pot's foreign minister during the "killing fields" years, and an estimated 4,000 dissident Khmer Rouge merged with government forces last week.
Ranariddh said the strategy of talks, not war, should be the way to bring about the end of Cambodia's decades-long war with the rebels.

"I think what we have to do is go through personal approaches. They do have their own colleagues, comrades-in-arms. We have to go through this way," the prince said at this one-time guerilla base in northwest Cambodia.

Ranariddh, who took pains to deny reports of fighting earlier this week between hardliners and government forces, said there was no breakthrough in talks on October 26 held in Thailand's Chonburi province.
Ei Chien, commander of Ieng Sary's forces in the northwest base of Pailin, said he, fellow Khmer Rouge dissident commander Sok Pheap and Ieng Vuth, son of Ieng Sary, all took part in the talks.
Ei Chien said he could not remember which hardliners attended but that they seemed unhappy about being there.
The Khmer Rouge have been fighting the government since being ousted from power by invading Vietnamese in 1979.
The Maoist group reneged on a 1991 U.N.-sponsored peace pact and continued a low-intensity campaign against the coalition government which came to power after elections in 1993.
